Refuting the Theory that the Effect Exists within the Cause (Part 2 of the Upper Section). This is the seventh section, "Refuting the Theory that the Effect Exists within the Cause.
The two pairs of the six sections have already been concluded. Now, we refute the third [position]: that there is both an effect and no effect. However—
The categories of identity and difference exhaust all possible ways of encompassing phenomena and sensory objects.
Whether the Great Existence (mahāsattā) is of one substance with things or of a different substance—
by refuting this duality of identity and difference, the teachings of external scriptures are shown to be empty.
The objects of the senses are the twelve bases (āyatana).
The twelve bases encompass all phenomena.
Since the objects of the senses are empty, then all things are empty.
If that is so, since the two pairs [of arguments] above have already exhausted the refutation of the dharmas,
there are now two further meanings— general and specific— to be refuted. Of these,
the general meaning has four points.
First, although the refutation of the higher [view] has exhausted the dharma, those of dull faculties have not yet attained realization;
therefore, it is established again and refuted once more.
Second, because their realizations differ, the gates of contemplation vary accordingly.
The two types of contemplative gates— namely,
that which is neither identical nor different, and neither internal nor external—
have already been clarified above. Now, we shall next explain the realization of the true nature (dharmatā) as being neither existent nor non-existent, and neither cause nor effect.
Third, the composition of treatises to harmonize with the sūtras.
Since the sūtras contain various divergent explanations,
the preceding two sections have already reconciled them through these two approaches.
Now, various Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the "Lion’s Roar" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, refute the notion that the effect exists within the cause.
Desiring to explain these sūtras, this present chapter is taught.
Fourth, this treatise primarily refutes external [schools] and secondarily refutes internal [schools].
From the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the eight hundredth year, the lineage split into five hundred sects.
Clinging to the notion that causes exist while effects do not, they obscured the Buddha’s sūtras.
Now, this chapter has been composed because [the author] refutes the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika,
as well as the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools.
Furthermore, there are four further meanings regarding its specific origination.
First, the "Spiritual Category" refutes persons, and the "Four Categories" refute dharmas.
Now, by citing cause and effect, we generally rescue both persons and dharmas.
Within the causes, the person is termed the "agent."
The person within the fruit is called the recipient;
the phenomena within the cause are precisely the wholesome and the unwholesome;
the phenomena within the fruit refer to suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Since cause and effect exist, persons and phenomena are not empty.
Second, this rescues from the aforementioned afflictions of the emotional senses;
each of these emotional objects has its own causes and effects.
For example, the arising of the great elements from atoms and the arising of the sense organs from the great elements refers to the causality of the sentient being (*sattva*).
The formation of form (*rūpa*) from atoms and the formation of a jar from form refers to the causality of the object (*viṣaya*).
Since causality exists, both the sentient being and the object are not empty.
Third, conditioned phenomena possess an essential nature and characteristics.
Cause and effect constitute the essential nature of conditioned phenomena,
while the three characteristics constitute the characteristics of the conditioned.
Since there are essential bodies and characteristics, there must be all phenomena;
how could there not be the objects of the senses?
Fourth, they arise in succession from one another, originating from the category of sense-objects.
The text clarifies this for itself.
Furthermore, regarding the arising of these two chapters, an external opponent says:
"Unity and difference cannot be apprehended either internally or externally."
Cause and effect constitute the great foundation of all meanings and the root for establishing faith; they cannot be said to be non-existent.
If they were non-existent, this would be a false view leading to rebirth in hell.
Therefore, cause and effect must exist.
Where there is cause and effect, there are internal and external, general and particular.
Where there are dharmas of internal and external, general and particular, there is the person.
Thus, everything is established.
Regarding the sequence of first refuting existence and subsequently refuting non-existence,
the general approach for both internal and external schools is the same. Internally, there are first those, such as the Sthaviras, who maintain that the three time periods exist.
Next, the great assembly considered that the two time periods do not exist.
Previously, the Abhidharma held that the two time periods exist;
subsequently, the *Tattvasiddhi* maintained that the two time periods do not exist.
The same applies to outsiders:
first there was Saṃkhya, who appeared in the world and asserted existence;
next came the Lokāyata teachers, who asserted non-existence.
Second, regarding the sequence of the four propositions:
there is the first, but not the second.
As for what is called "refuting the existence of the effect within the cause":
Regarding the ninety-six arts enumerated in the *Daming* (Great Illumination), there are three [categories].
The first is the adherence to the view that there is neither cause nor effect;
for example, as one teacher among the six masters said:
There is no black karma and no retribution for black karma;
the same applies to white [karma] and so forth.
Second, they maintain that there is fruit without a cause.
Among the six teachers, there were also such persons as these.
Three maintained that causes and effects exist;
regarding these causes and effects, there were further four teachers.
First, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the effect exists within the cause;
second, the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the effect does not exist within the cause;
third, the Ājīvikas maintain both existence and non-existence.
Fourth, the son of Ajita [Pūraṇa Kāśyapa] maintains that things neither exist nor do not exist.
Within the Buddha-dharma, both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna clarify the principle of cause and effect.
Among these, within the Hīnayāna, there is the Sāṃkhya school.
Regarding the six causes and five fruits mentioned by some:
as for the six causes, they are:
first, the associated cause; second, the coexistent cause; third, the retributive cause; fourth, the pervasive cause; fifth, the homogeneous cause; and sixth, the efficient cause.
Regarding the five fruits:
first, the fruit of liberation arises from the Truth of the Path;
if one speaks in terms of its causal basis.
They also exist by virtue of the cause of action (*kāraṇahetu*),
yet only the six causes directly produce conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
The fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is not produced by the six causes.
The remaining four fruits arise from six causes.
The dominant fruit arises from the homogeneous cause and the pervasive cause;
the retributive fruit arises from the retributive cause.
The associated and coexistent causes produce the fruit of activity;
the efficient cause produces the sovereign fruit.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, these three causes and four conditions comprise two types of cause and effect.
If the two causes— the habitual cause and the retributive cause— arise sequentially,
there is nevertheless the principle that cause and effect can also exist simultaneously,
as in the case of the first moment of ignorance according to the *Arthaviniścaya-śāstra*.
If cause and effect exist simultaneously based on their mutual dependence, this is the principle of simultaneous causal conditioning (*sahabhū-pratyaya*),
such as the five aggregates forming a person or the four atoms forming a pillar, which exist at one and the same time.
To state it broadly:
those who hold the view that both time periods exist maintain that the effect exists within the cause;
those who argue that both time periods do not exist clarify that the effect does not exist within the cause.
Regarding the Mahāyāna clarification of cause and effect, as explained in the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* (Dìchí lùn), there are ten causes and five effects.
The five effects are identical in number, meaning, and name [to those in other systems].
The ten causes are as described in that treatise.
However, those of the Mahāyāna understand that regarding the supramundane cause and effect, there are two kinds of permanence: the future and the present.
They clarify that within the midst of birth and death, the Dharma-body and its attributes are already fully complete;
because this meaning of being manifest and permanent, it is termed "existence."
Because it is obscured by delusion and does not manifest, it is termed "without fruit.
Regarding the meaning of "should be":
that which is destined to have a fruit is termed "having the meaning [of existence]."
If it has not yet arisen, it cannot be called "without fruit.
[The opponent] asks: "Now you refute the externalist view of cause and effect;
why then do you analyze the causes and effects of both the mundane and supramundane realms?"
Answer: If the Lion’s Roar uses milk and curd as a metaphor to discuss the Buddha-nature, what prevents Deva from using clay jars to distinguish the causes and effects of the Dharma-body?
Thus, both the mundane and the supramundane are entirely correct.
Transcending the world is itself the Buddha-nature.
If the Buddha-nature is correct, then the nature of the Buddha is correct.
If the nature of the Buddha is correct, then the Three Jewels are correct.
Therefore, the matter of cause and effect is great, and it is for this reason that we discuss it. Question:
Why is it that [the opponent] specifically refutes the existence of the effect within the cause?
Answer: Because it is the middle way that is free from the extremes of existence and non-existence; because it is the root of all views;
and because sentient beings cling to it excessively.
This is because they are prevalent in the world.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya school holds the thesis that the effect exists within the cause among its twenty-five principles (*tattva*),
while the Vaiśeṣika school holds the thesis that the effect does not exist within the cause among its six categories (*padārtha*).
Now, if their great root is destroyed, the branches will naturally fall away.
This chapter is divided into four sections.
First, the refutation of the outsider’s claim that there is no loss of the self.
Second, refuting the argument that the cause proves the existence of the effect by means of their being raised together;
third, refuting the argument that the cause proves the existence of the effect by means of their being taken separately;
fourth, refuting the opponent's erroneous claim that this establishes the view of annihilationism.
The opponent says: "It is not the case that all phenomena do not abide.
This is established with three intentions:
first, to refute the proponent; second, to establish one's own thesis; and third, to refute the Vaiśeṣika.
In the latter part of the superior grade, all phenomena arise and perish from moment to moment without a time of abiding.
Because the external party now refutes the internal [position] with these words, it is said that they do not "not abide.
Since there is no loss [of the phenomenon], this constitutes the second established tenet of our own school.
The cause transforms into the fruit without losing its causal nature.
The reason for clarifying "non-loss" (avipraṇāśa) is that it constitutes the primary tenet of the twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva) of the Sāṃkhya school.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes that teaching as saying:
"From darkness arises awakening, and so on, up to the arising of the sense faculties from the great elements.
This means that from the subtle, the coarse arises.
The faculties disperse back into the great elements, and even from awakening they return to obscurity;
that is to say, they proceed from the coarse back to the subtle.
Although they emerge from the subtle into the coarse and return from the coarse to the subtle, there is ultimately nothing lost.
Therefore, the establishment of existence serves to prevent the loss of meaning.
Furthermore, citing "existence" as a proof prevents the fallacy of non-abiding.
Since there is nothing that does not arise, this refutes the Vātsīputrīyas.
This does not mean that it is not non-abiding.
The commentary explains the latter two lines by dividing them into four distinct parts.
First, it explains "existence without loss" (yǒu bùshī) in order to refute the internal fallacy.
The section beginning with "If the effect does not exist within the cause" criticizes the Lokāyata teachers.
By asserting that the cause transforms into the effect, it anticipates the objections of both the Sāṃkhya (Devaputra) and the Lokāyata schools:
if the cause is not lost, how can the effect arise?
Therefore, the commentary explains that the cause transforms into the effect;
thus, while the effect arises, the essence of the effect is identical to the essence of the cause,
and so there is no loss.
Therefore, there exist various dharmas, such as the fourth realization, sentient beings, objects, and identity or difference.
The internal [text] states that by refuting the superior [position] below, the inferior is not lost.
There are two original verses.
If the effect arises, it exists; this refutes the external position that [the cause] is not lost.
Because the cause is lost, there is loss; this is the internal refutation.
Because the effect arises, the effect exists.
Therefore, the fruit exists without being lost;
because the cause is lost, there would be no cause.
If the cause exists, it ought to be lost.
Furthermore, loss and non-loss are mutually relative, just as cause and effect are.
Since the effect is not lost, the cause must be lost.
Moreover, if the cause were not lost simultaneously with it, the effect would not arise.
If the fruit were to arise, the cause would be lost.
Furthermore, since the cause does not perish, the cause must remain unchanging;
if it were to change, it would be lost.
Furthermore, if there were no loss, then cause and effect would not be distinct.
Since cause and effect are indeed distinct, there must be loss.
This note first restates the opponent’s position regarding non-loss.
The jar is precisely the lump of clay in the process of being destroyed.
There are four difficulties [to be addressed];
the first is the difficulty regarding its initial production.
If the jar arises as a distinct effect, there is the second objection regarding the loss of the cause.
If the lump of clay does not lose its nature, there is the third objection regarding the non-differentiation of the product.

Now, when one actually perceives differences in shape, temporal power, cognition, and so forth, there is the fourth objection, which uses the evidence of these five distinct factors to refute the claim of non-difference.
Regarding the five points:
first, the clay vessel has two distinct forms;
that is to say, the form of the clay ceases and the form of the vessel arises.
This refers to the loss of form.
Second, at the time of the clay, the jar ceases; at that time, [the jar] arises.
Third, by the power of the clay, the power of the jar ceases, and [the power of the jar] arises.
Fourth, when the cognition of clay ceases, the cognition of a jar arises.
Fifth, the name "clay" ceases and the name "jar" arises.
The opponent says: "Just as a finger is bent and extended, this rescues [the argument] from the fault of the previous reason's loss of meaning."
Externally, one need not necessarily speak; it may suffice merely to move a finger.
For example, as the Dharma Master in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* relates, when a king raised difficulties regarding the five precepts, the master answered him by raising his finger.
The present case is likewise.
Although the finger changes its form when bent or extended, the substance of the finger is not lost.
It is like a clay jar: although its shape differs, its essential nature does not differ.
Furthermore, above it was argued that the reason (*hetu*) is lost because of the five points of difference;
yet here, although there are also five points of difference, the finger is not lost.
[The opponent] asks: For what reason does the externalist raise the finger as a refutation?
The answer has three points:
first, the matter is visible in the present;
second, it does not necessarily require verbal expression, as a mere movement of the finger suffices.
Regarding the three great luminances (*mahāvidyā*), there are two dharmas that are non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*).
What has been explained above was the non-perishing of external things such as jars;
from here onward, we shall explain the non-perishing of internal [dharmas].
Among internal phenomena (*ādhyātmika-dharma*), there are two:
first, specifically designated phenomena; second, youth, adulthood, and old age.
These two collectively encompass all internal things without exception.
The internal [opponent] says: "That is not so, because karma is capable of differentiation.
Bending, stretching, moving, and shaking are the karmas of the body;
"capable" refers to the substance [of the body].
The reason the substance is designated as "the capable" is that the finger is called "capable" because it can bend and extend; yet,
the finger is distinct from the acts of bending and extending.
Your "nature" (svabhāva) is not different from the clay pot;
one should not employ a dissimilar example for that which is non-different.
If the bending and extending were not different from the finger, there would be seven difficulties.
First, by following the bending and extending of the fingers,
when the fingers are one, the bending and extending are one.
Second, by following the bending and extending with the fingers.
If bending and extending constitute two [distinct acts], then the two fingers should likewise be two [distinct entities].
Yet, when three fingers bend or extend, they do not become three;
thus, the fingers must be distinct from the acts of bending and extending.
Fourth, if the bending and extending are not identical to the two fingers,
then the bending and extending would be distinct from the fingers.
Fifth, if one wishes for them to be a single entity yet not conform to one another, one falls into the error of being both identical and different.
This has already been explained above.
Regarding the sixth [point], extension and contraction are identical to the finger:
when there is contraction, there is no longer extension; and at the time of contraction, the finger itself should not exist.
If the finger still exists at the time of bending, then at the time of bending it must also exist at the time of stretching.
Thus, the seven acts of bending and stretching would be identical to the single finger; the single finger would be the two states of bending and stretching.
It should also follow that bending and extending [the fingers] would be identical to bending one finger or two; for bending and extending are one and the same.
The opponent says: This is like the difficulty raised regarding the difference in capacity for performing superior deeds among the young, the middle-aged, and the old;
although there are differences between youth, middle age, and old age, they are ultimately one and the same person.
Although there is a difference between bending and extending, they are ultimately one finger;
although there is a difference between an earthen jar and a clay jar, they are ultimately one substance.
According to the masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, because the beginning and end are continuously linked, they are ultimately one person.
Therefore, at the initial moment of entering the womb, one is called a person of name-and-form;
subsequently, one is called a person of the five aggregates,
continuing through the stages of youth, maturity, and old age.
Furthermore, just as the mind and the eyes are the sovereign, so it is with the Buddha; they are not different, only their names differ.
The *Vibhāṣā* presents two types of treatises.
1. The theory that the nature of a single entity undergoes transformation:
this asserts that because youth transforms into old age, the beginning and end constitute one and the same person.
2. The theory that the nature of an existing entity comes and goes.
It is not that the cloud changes from youth to old age;
rather, as youth passes, one enters into old age.
Therefore, an old person remembers the events of their youth.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"These are all the meanings of the eight heterodoxies and were not spoken by the Buddha.
Regarding the internal [objection] that "they are not one," this refutes the previous claim that the old and the young are of a single essence.
That is to say, the five factors—youthful form, name, power, cognition, and time—cease before [old age], and the five factors of old age arise afterward.
How could these be a single entity?
If they were a single entity, old age should possess all five factors of youth.
If that is so, then what is it that is called "old" within the "young"?
There should likewise be five difficulties and three barriers;
youth, old age, and the person are one and the same.
If the person is one, then the old and the young are one.
If the person is one with the old and the young,
then if the old and the young are different, the person must be different.
This can be understood from the preceding examples.
Furthermore, if there were such a thing as non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*), this would entail two types of production: proximate and remote.
Dharmapāla refutes the fundamental tenets of that [Samkhya] school:
"Your twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are all existent entities (*dharmin*).
Although they proceed from the subtle to the gross and from the gross to the subtle, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is never lost."
That which exists is not lost;
space is a non-phenomenon,
and within non-existence there is no loss.
If that is so, there is no loss whatsoever in the world;
since "loss" was established only in contrast to "gain," when loss itself is absent, [gain] cannot exist either.
Therefore, even "attainment" does not exist.
Second, from the preceding section onward, the specific clarification that internal and external phenomena are without loss has been concluded;
now, the fault of [claiming] that both the internal and external are without loss is demonstrated in general.
The third section refutes the arising of old age and death.
At the time of old age, this "existence" (bhāva) does not lose [its nature];
in the absence of old age, there is nothing that is lost.
The refutation of this view is the same as before.
As for the commentary stating that "a lump of clay should not transform into a jar," this too constitutes a parallel argument.
If there is no loss, there is no change;
if there is change, there is loss.
Furthermore, these two are refuted through mutual opposition.
If there is non-loss when there is presence, there is no loss when there is absence. Since there is already no loss when there is presence, there should likewise be no loss when there is absence.
The opponent says: What fault is there in this non-loss?
The twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva) possess an enduring nature;
because this is their primary tenet, it is not considered a fault.
The commentary states: "The lump of clay does not undergo transformation to become the jar."
Master Feng said:
"Vasubandhu was too extreme in his arguments against the outsiders;
they merely state that because there is transformation, there is no loss."
It is not because of immutability that there is no loss.
Now, a single principle is clarified:
first, above, it was shown that through immutability there is no loss.
The case of the non-Buddhists being stalled and subsequently converting their sects is analogous.
There are two types of transformation:
first, transformation through the loss and extinction of names.
The second [kind of change] is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
What is here termed "unchanging" refers to the absence of the change of destruction;
therefore, the text says there is no impermanence (*anityatā*).
This is known through verification.
The internal [objection] states: "If there were no impermanence, there would be no demerit, merit, and so forth; this would refute the previously established principle of non-loss.
Since demerit would not be lost, demerit would be permanent; therefore, there would be no merit.
Merit is also like this.
Furthermore, if there were no impermanence, there would be no permanence, and thus everything would be non-existent.
Moreover, if there were no loss, afflictions could never be eliminated, and one could never attain liberation.
Furthermore, if sin were not lost and merit were not produced, then all phenomena would be like space—neither arising nor ceasing.
The opponent says: "The effect pre-exists within the cause."
From the beginning up to this point, the first [section] has primarily refuted the grand thesis of the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), clarifying the principle that nothing is lost.
Now, the second [section] correctly refutes the position that the effect pre-exists within the cause.
Now, the opponent previously raised the reason that there is evidence for the existence of the effect within the cause;
if the effect were non-existent, it would not differ from what is not a cause.
Since there is now a cause, it differs from what is not a cause.
Since there is no effect in the absence of a cause,
it is verified that the effect already exists within the cause;
as some [schools] say, "the cause possesses the nature of the effect."
The treatise states that while the principle of the cause having the effect is different [from it], the principle of non-nature is not.
Regarding the internal [refutation] below, there are two parts:
first, the restatement; second, the refutation.

If one argues that the effect exists because it is already present within the cause—this cites the opponent's position—the response is that since the effect does not exist, the cause cannot have an effect; this is the subsequent refutation.
You truly do not see the effect existing within the cause.
One merely observes that the effect arises from the cause.
If one were to claim that the effect already exists within the cause,
then one should likewise observe the destruction of the jar-effect at a later time.
One should say that the effect does not exist within the cause.
If one sees the destruction of the effect, one does not say it was absent from the cause;
likewise, if one sees the formation of the effect, one does not say it was present in the cause.
Furthermore, the examples all state:
"If one observes that something is absent at a later time but was present within the cause earlier,
then one must also observe that what exists later was absent within the cause."
Furthermore, if it were not the case that [the effect] is absent within the cause, but rather becomes absent at a later time,
then that which exists spontaneously would also necessarily exist as something that arises spontaneously.
Moreover, if this [effect] were originally non-existent within the cause and only subsequently became non-existent, [it would follow that it arose from nothing].
Furthermore, it is because this [effect] was originally non-existent within the cause, yet comes into existence later.
The opponent says: Since cause and effect are one, this refutes the position that the effect does not exist within the cause.
I maintain that the essence of cause and effect is identical.
The cause is destroyed by the effect;
since there is no such thing as an uncaused [destruction],
the effect is now destroyed.
How could it be that there is no fruit?
It is like transforming clay into a jar—the jar does not lose its nature as earth;
or transforming a jar into earth—the jar is likewise not lost.
Although the processes of formation and destruction differ, the principle that [the effect] is always present remains constant;
therefore, it is not the case that the effect does not exist within the cause.
The internal [opponent] says: "If cause and effect were one, there would be no future; this refutes the position that cause and effect are one."
When clarifying the time of the clay, the jar is originally considered the future;
because the clay is itself the jar, there is no future [jar].
When grasping the jar in relation to the clay, the clay becomes the past.
The clay jar itself is also without past;
furthermore, one regards the clay as the "past" in relation to the jar,
yet since the jar is nothing other than the clay, there is no past or future.

The opponent says: Because the loss of a name gives rise to another name, and because a name arises from the loss of a name, there are three time periods; this is a general objection applicable to both [the internal and external].
Since the substance has neither arising nor loss, cause and effect are not different.
One's own school's position is thereby established.
The commentary asks: "Where are the jars and pots?
To which it replies: "The substance of the jars and pots remains just as it is."
This means that if the substance (*tattva*) does not perish, then the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established.
However, because there is the loss of the name (*nāman*), there is the establishment of the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*) based on whether [the entity] exists or does not exist.
The internal [opponent] says: "If that were so, there would be no fruit (*phala*)."
Refuting the aforementioned [position] means that while there is the production of loss regarding the name, there is no production of loss regarding the substance (*tattva*).
There are generally two difficulties:
first, the difficulty of grasping the substance by means of the name.
Fundamentally, the name summons the essence and the essence responds to the name.
If the essence of the fruit existed previously, it should have responded to the name of the fruit existing previously;
if the name of the fruit did not exist previously, then the essence of the fruit likewise did not exist previously.
Second, if within the cause the name "effect" does not exist prior [to its production], then the name and the entity must be one and the same thing.
Since the name "effect" does not exist prior within the cause,
it follows that the effect does not exist within the cause.
The opponent says: "Because it is indeterminate. This is a rebuttal to the previous objection that the effect does not exist within the cause.

The reason why the essence of the effect exists within the cause prior to its establishment, yet the name "effect" is not yet applied, is that within the cause, any single vessel may emerge indeterminately.
Therefore, the name has not yet been applied to that which is to become the fruit;
thus, although the name does not exist, the substance of the fruit does.
The internal [proponent] says: If the clay is not fixed, the fruit is also not fixed.
"If the clay is indeterminate" cites the opponent's position;
"the result is also indeterminate" is the actual refutation.
As for your claim that because it is indeterminate it cannot produce a single object, and therefore it cannot be designated as a jar and thus lacks a name—[this is incorrect].
Furthermore, it should not be established as having the fixed meaning of being a single entity,
nor should it be considered indeterminate.
The reason it is indeterminate is that this clay may become a jar or it may become some other object.
The opponent says: "Because subtle forms exist.
This means that since subtle forms definitely exist within the clay, their existence is certain.
Although they are not seen by the fleshly eye, they are seen by the divine eye; thus, when one sees the future, one sees the subtle forms within the clay.
The commentary is divided into three parts:
first, explaining the root verse to clarify that there is indeed a fixed [nature], which contains two kinds of unknowables; second, preventing objections.
The objection states:
Since it is a subtle form, by what means can it be known?
Since it cannot be known, how can one say that it exists?
Therefore, it is now clarified that two things are unknowable,
while one thing is not unknowable;
for example, one cannot know a rabbit's horn.
Second, there is that which cannot be known, which is similar to the eight conditions.
Thus, within the lump of clay, the pot [is not perceived]; this is the third instance of citing a non-cause to infer the existence of the cause within the effect.
In short, [an effect] emerges from a cause and does not emerge from what is not a cause.
Since that which is not a cause does not exist, one knows that the cause exists.
The internal [opponent] says: "If there was previously a subtle form, yet the effect is not present within the cause..."
This [argument] concedes that while the subtle exists,
the coarse does not; one should know, therefore, that the coarse effect was originally non-existent and now exists.
Furthermore, if the subtle exists while the coarse does not, then it would both exist and not exist,
which is identical to the doctrine of the Leśa-bha (Jainas).
Moreover, if the coarse does not exist within the cause, then the coarse effect would arise from what is not its cause.
Furthermore, if your position holds that the subtle is necessarily determined, it should also have a determined cause.
If there is a subtle [cause] within, it should in turn produce a subtle effect.
Moreover, if the coarse and the subtle were not determinate, their existence would likewise not be determinate.
Furthermore, if the effect already exists within the cause, then both the coarse and the subtle must exist simultaneously, and thus they should arise simultaneously.
Moreover, if the coarse arises while the subtle does not, then the coarse would exist while the subtle would not.

The opponent says: "The effect must exist within the cause, because one apprehends each individual cause. This is the third refutation of the opponent's argument that the existence of the effect is proven by the apprehension of individual causes.
The difference from the second section above is this:
the former directly clarifies that because the cause exists, one proves the existence of the effect;
this [section], however, distinguishes the cause from what is not a cause.
Now, to clarify the individual appropriation of causes, we shall distinguish them by means of their causes.
Since the various causes produce fruits that are each distinct, this proves that the fruit exists within the cause.
If the effect were not present within the cause, then all causes would produce effects in a disordered manner,
and effects would likewise arise from causes in a disordered fashion; yet, in reality, causes do not produce effects in a disordered way, nor do effects arise from causes in a disordered way.
This verifies that the effect is definitively present within the cause.
The commentary states: "Molding clay into vessels makes them fit to undergo firing.
The *Benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin) says:
"Kneading clay to make it supple" refers to mixing mud.
The "Outer Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*, in the "Horse's Hoof" (*Mati*) section, states: "Gently treating the clay."
Sima Biao’s commentary states:
"Zhi" refers to clay;
it is that which can be fashioned into vessels.
In the "Yugong" (Tribute of Yu) chapter of the Book of Documents, "red clay" (*chizhi*) is also referred to as "earth" (*tu*).
The character *ni* means "harmony";
it refers simply to the softening and working of the soil with one's hands.
That wheel is called the "pivot" (gūn).

The internal [argument] states: "If there were existence, it would be 'when there ought to be existence'; if there were non-existence, it would be 'when there ought to be non-existence. This refutes the former [position] by taking the cause as the evidence to prove that the effect exists within the cause.
What distinguishes this from the previous refutation is as follows:
Above, it was clarified that one sees with the eyes a jar emerging from clay,
which serves as evidence that the effect exists within the cause.
Likewise, one also sees with the eyes a jar being broken, which implies that the effect does not exist within the cause.
This has been an examination based on the present state of the cause, whether it exists or not at the time of destruction.
Now, we shall refute [the opponent's position] from the perspective of the future state:
your effect is not something presently existing; it must necessarily be something that will exist in the future.
A pot within the clay possesses both the sense of being about to be formed and the sense of being about to be broken.
If one were to say that the effect exists within the cause because the pot within the clay has the sense of being about to be formed,
then since the pot within the cause also has the sense of being about to be broken, it would likewise follow that there is no effect.
Second, whereas previously the refutation was based on the nature (*tattva*) of arising and destruction, here the refutation is based on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The opponent says:
"Since there is a sequential occurrence of arising, abiding, and destruction, there is no fault; this answers the objection raised above that [the entity] would necessarily be non-existent."
Although a jar within the clay has both the state of being formed and the state of being destroyed,
the state of being formed exists prior to the state of being destroyed, and the state of being destroyed exists subsequent to the state of being formed.
Because the state of being formed comes first, and we follow that priority, it is said that "that which is to be" exists within the cause.
Since the refutation has already been established above, how can one now claim from a subsequent perspective that the effect does not exist within the cause?
This is like citing the sequence of arising, abiding,
and decaying as an analogy for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It must be that arising comes first, followed by abiding, and finally destruction.
When the jar is in the process of arising, since it has not yet reached the stages of formation and destruction, what object could there be to destroy the jar? Is the jar not present right now?
The Dārṣṭāntikas clarify that three moments constitute the three characteristics.
At the time when the first moment arises, abiding and decay do not yet exist.
This is consistent with that meaning.
According to the Satyasiddhi masters, the three characteristics of real dharmas exist within a single thought-moment of sixty *kṣaṇas*.
Of these, the first twenty constitute arising (*jāti*).
The next twenty constitute abiding;
the final twenty constitute cessation.
It is the same for these as well.
The internal [proponent] says: If it were non-existent prior to arising, there would be no result; this equally refutes the aforementioned sequence of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
A jar within the clay possesses only its impending arising, but not yet its impending abiding or impending cessation.
Thus, since the two characteristics of abiding and ceasing do not exist within the cause,
there is no correspondence with the effect.
These two characteristics of abiding and ceasing are themselves the effect.
Since there are no two distinct characteristics, it is called "without effect.
Furthermore, the jar within the clay possesses all three characteristics;
yet you claim that the cause contains the effect based solely on the presence of the characteristic of arising.
Since the two characteristics of abiding and ceasing do not exist,
there should be no effect within the cause;
furthermore, since the three characteristics are mutually dependent, if abiding and ceasing are absent, [the other characteristics cannot exist].
For what purpose would one speak of arising?
Therefore, there is no arising; since the three characteristics do not exist, there is no essence of phenomena.
Thus, the effect does not exist within the cause.
Furthermore, at the time of arising, abiding and ceasing do not yet exist;
thus, if the essence of a phenomenon lacks these three characteristics, it is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then such a thing does not exist at all.
Furthermore, there is no effect within the cause.
This is divided into two parts.
First, the refutation of the three characteristics occurring simultaneously.
This immediately refutes the doctrines of the Abhidharma and other schools.
If you claim that the three characteristics of a jar exist simultaneously within the clay while it is yet in the future,
why must its arising necessarily precede its destruction rather than its destruction preceding its arising?

Your statement that "because [the effect] has not yet arisen" constitutes the second section below, which refutes the priority and posteriority of the three characteristics and thereby refutes the logic of the analogies and so forth. The opponent says:

"Because you refute the existence of the effect within the cause, there is the fault of annihilationism"; this is the fourth section, where the proponent refutes the opponent’s groundless accusations.
Now, the externalist's error exceeds that of the internalist.
First, they perceive the principle of cause and effect as not transcending existence and non-existence;
having already perceived the refutation of existence within the internalist's view, they consequently claim that the internalist clings to non-existence.
Second, borrowing "non-existence" from above to refute "existence," which refers to the internal clinging to non-existence:
if the effect does not exist within the cause, then the effect will not arise;
since the effect does not arise, there is no continuity of the arising of an effect.
Therefore, it is called "severing.
Third, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Sentient beings give rise to views in two general ways."
One is annihilationism and the other is eternalism.
The former attachment to existence constitutes eternalism;
now, by abandoning that eternalism, one enters into annihilationism.
This is because any attainment based on the notion of "something to be gained" must necessarily rely upon [a substrate].
The internal [position] states: Because it continues, it is not annihilated; because it does not undergo destruction, it is not eternal.
By virtue of its continuity, it is not annihilated; this refutes the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Because it is subject to destruction, it is not eternal; thus, their view of permanence is refuted.
Since they previously clung to the view of annihilationism, that annihilationism was first refuted, lest, by removing annihilationism, they should fall back into permanence.
Therefore, the refutation of permanence follows next.
An old [commentary] also says:
"In reality there is cessation and no permanence, yet through conventional continuity there is no interruption."
How does this differ from the present [position]?
Answer: That doctrine holds that while things truly cease and are not eternal, they are nonetheless subject to annihilation;
yet because there is continuity, they are not annihilated, which is thus equivalent to the meaning of permanence.
Therefore, one clings to permanence as being non-interruption and clings to annihilation as being non-permanence;
thus, annihilation and permanence exist in mutual dependence.
This is merely the meaning of annihilationism and eternalism.
Now it is clarified that these two are both refuted and not both accepted.
To say that it is not eternal means:
To clarify that it is not permanent does not mean that it is impermanent;
the same applies to its non-interruption.

Furthermore, it has often been said that true cessation is not permanence, while conventional continuity is not interruption; thus, being free from both annihilation and permanence, there is arising and ceasing.
Now it is clarified that since there is neither annihilation nor permanence, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"To seek deeply that which is neither eternal nor annihilated is precisely that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, although the older [tradition] clarifies non-annihilation and non-eternality, it still clings to the notion that there is no meaning in the two periods [of past and future].
Several people hold the view that there is existence in both past and future lives through the principle of neither annihilation nor permanence.
Now it is clarified that this "neither annihilation nor permanence" means neither non-existence nor existence;
this is explicitly stated in the commentary.
Question: For what reason does the Master of the Treatise [assert that] it is continuous, not subject to interruption or destruction, and not eternal?
Answer: It is said that if one examines its beginning and end, there are two refutations [of such claims].
First, refutation by means of conditions (*pratyaya*):
for example, when one investigates existence based on grasping at existence, one finds that there is no source from which it arises.
Second, refutation by means of confronting conditions.
There are two ways of refuting through conditions:
first, using non-existence to refute existence and using the false to refute the false;
second, presenting the correct to refute the false.
This refers precisely to the present passage.
Beyond this, [the views] do not transcend [the positions of] existence or non-existence within the cause;
"existence" implies permanence, while "non-existence" implies annihilationism.

Now, by confronting existence and non-existence, as well as annihilation and permanence, it is clarified that [the Middle Way] is neither existent nor non-existent, and neither annihilated nor permanent;
thus, this Middle Way is elucidated through its contrast with extremes.
Question: Since it continues, it is not annihilated; since it does not disintegrate, it is not permanent. How, then, is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Answer: Because it continues, it is not interrupted; this refutes [the view] that the cause is non-existent.
Because it disintegrates, it is not eternal; this refutes [the view] that the cause is existent.
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the effect exists within the cause.
This is because the cause is not lost or destroyed. 8.

Refuting the Absence of the Fruit within the Cause (Part 1 of 2). Chapter Eight: Refuting the Absence of the Fruit within the Cause. The fundamental dualistic attachments to existence and non-existence held by the two schools—the internal and external—[are as follows].
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that [the self] exists, while the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that it does not.
The Sthaviras maintain that it exists, while the Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that it does not.
The former [argument] primarily refutes the existence held by outsiders, while incidentally refuting the existence held by those within [the Buddhist fold].
Now, this primarily refutes the "non-existence" of external objects and secondarily refutes the "non-existence" of internal consciousness.
This is because existence and non-existence are the roots of manifold views and obstacles to the fundamental Middle Way;
therefore, they must be washed away.
Furthermore, previously you refuted the existence of the Sāṃkhya school; now you have changed your position and grasped at non-existence.
Therefore, I shall refute this non-existence.
Moreover, previously you relied upon non-existence to refute existence.
Thus, there exists that which is to be refuted, but there is no refuter.
Previously, the object of refutation was refuted; now, the refuter is refuted.
Furthermore, by refuting the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the existence [of the conditioned] is eliminated.
Existence and non-existence are mutually dependent phenomena;
if one does not negate non-existence, the view of existence will arise once more.
Therefore, by negating non-existence, one causes the mind’s preoccupation with existence to completely cease.
Furthermore, this chapter primarily refutes arising and does not refute non-existence;
it merely refutes non-existence for the sake of countering the Sāṃkhya position of existence.
Question: Why is arising refuted?
Answer: Deva’s treatise refuting conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) generally employs four gates.
The first is the gate of refuting the ultimate oneness by means of the fruit of existence to refute the essence of the conditioned.
This chapter is the gate for refuting the characteristics of the conditioned.
Once the essence and characteristics are eliminated, all conditioned phenomena are exhausted;
therefore, it refutes arising.
Second, the author of the treatise generally refutes two categories of phenomena by concluding with their identity or difference.
Based on the existence of the cause, he refutes distinct phenomena—
that is, those variously conceived differently by different schools.
Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the specific nature of phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, we shall next refute their commonality.
The three characteristics are termed "common" because they are common to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, it is called "universal" because it is established by all teachers;
therefore, it refutes arising.
Thirdly, it is intended to demonstrate that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and are likewise unceasing now.
This causes the non-Buddhists to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, there is no arising.

Fourth, at the end of the "Superior Chapter" (*uttara-pakṣa*), the master of the treatise borrows the arising of the fruit to refute their views of annihilationism and eternalism by means of the cessation of the cause.
Although the views of annihilationism and eternalism have been eliminated, the affliction of arising and ceasing immediately arises.
As others say: "In reality, there is cessation and thus no permanence; through conventional continuity, there is no interruption.
Thus, although there is neither annihilation nor permanence, there is still arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is now clarified that since there is neither annihilation nor permanence, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Consequently, arising and ceasing are next refuted.
The preceding refutation of annihilation and permanence was the refutation of the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Now, this chapter is composed in order to refute the doctrines of the internal schools by dismantling the notions of both provisional and real arising and ceasing.
This chapter consists of five sections.
First, it refutes the opponent’s argument that the existence of a productive cause can be proven by means of the producible effect.
Second, it refutes the opponent’s argument that the existence of the producible effect can be proven by means of the productive cause.
Third, it refutes the opponent’s argument that the existence of all phenomena can be proven by citing both the producer and the produced together.
The fourth [section] refutes the proof that there is the meaning of arising through the act of censuring;
the fifth refutes the proof that there is the meaning of arising and being able to arise by citing cause and effect.
The opponent says: "Because arising exists, one must necessarily be established."
The phrase "because there is arising" refers to the Master’s preceding statement that the continuum is uninterrupted.
Because the cause ceases, it is not eternal; because the fruit arises, it is not annihilated.
You, however, do not establish [the Middle Way] by avoiding annihilationism and eternalism, yet you nonetheless posit the existence of arising and ceasing.
If one posits that there is arising and ceasing, then one is the same as myself.

This is precisely because the Sāṃkhya school and those Mahāyānists who hold to objective attainment clarify that conditioned phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal, yet they possess arising and ceasing; thus it is said, "because arising exists."
Regarding "the first being established":
previously the characteristic of arising was established, and now the substantial entity (dharmatā) is established. Since the characteristic of arising already exists, [the entity follows].
Among the four positions—whether the effect exists in the cause, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist—one must necessarily hold to one of them.
The proponent says: "Arising is non-arising; it does not arise."
Previously, by borrowing the refutation of arising and ceasing, we demolished [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism.
One who has profound awakening neither clings to annihilationism and eternalism nor clings to arising and ceasing.
However, those of middling or inferior faculties with dull roots, while not clinging to annihilationism and eternalism, further cling to arising and ceasing.
Now, this section refutes arising and ceasing.
This verse originally possesses two meanings.
As for what is called "arising":
This means that the effect exists prior to the cause;
"non-arising" means that the effect does not exist prior to the cause.
These two [statements] cite that one [point] which should be established.
Regarding "non-arising":

it clarifies that the characteristic of arising cannot produce either an effect with existence or an effect without existence; therefore, both effects with existence and those without existence are equally non-arising.
This refers to the phrase "because it destroys that existence of birth.
This interpretation is merely a forceful refutation;
it is not the intended meaning of the original text.
Furthermore, looking ahead at the subsequent explanation:
that which "arises" already possesses the substance of a dharma;
that which "does not arise" has not yet acquired the substance of a dharma.
That which is unarisen does not arise through the characteristic of arising.
These two types of dharmas already possess their own substance and do not require the characteristic of arising;
if they do not yet exist, the characteristic of arising cannot produce them.
Next it says:
"Arising" clarifies that the characteristic of arising already exists;
"non-arising" means that the characteristic of arising does not yet exist.
That which has not yet arisen—whether it possesses the characteristic of arising or does not yet possess the characteristic of arising—is incapable of producing the essence of a dharma.
How can you claim that because arising exists, the one [dharma] must necessarily be established?
This interpretation is correct.
Since the opponent correctly cites the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) as proof for the existence of the substance of a phenomenon (*dharma-svabhāva*),
[the author] therefore correctly refutes the characteristic of arising by clarifying that it cannot produce the substance of a phenomenon.

Furthermore, for those such as the Vaibhāṣikas, who hold that there is a characteristic of arising (utpāda-lakṣaṇa) existing separately outside the essence of the dharma itself; whereas for those who hold there is no [separate arising],
there is no characteristic of arising existing separately outside the essence of the dharma itself.
This is analogous to the case of the *dharma-śramaṇa*.
Furthermore, those who assert that the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
such as the followers of the Sāṃkhya school.
Those who hold the view of non-arising (anutpāda) reckon that the characteristic of arising is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is like the school of the Vibhajyavādins and others;
for them, both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, being distinct from the phenomenon itself, are incapable of producing the essence of a phenomenon.
The *Wenju* contains this intention for refutation.
The commentary divides it into two parts.
First, it addresses how the presence or absence of arising-characteristics cannot produce the essence of a dharma.
Next, it is explained that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) cannot produce because it lacks the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
Since Vasubandhu held these two perspectives, the preceding [section] provided two interpretations.
If there were such an arising, [it would be as follows].
This cites the word "arises" from the root verse.
By stating "prior to the cause" and "not prior to the cause," this explains the word "does not arise" in the root verse.
Even if you grant that there is a characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
If the effect already exists within the cause, it does not need to be produced by the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
If the effect is previously non-existent within the cause, the characteristic of arising cannot produce it.
Therefore, there is no characteristic of arising.
How much more so for that which is "non-arising"— a term explained in the commentary on the root verse as "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).
Since even that which possesses the characteristic of arising cannot produce the essence of a phenomenon (dharma-svabhāva) when there is neither a cause nor a fruit,
how much less can that which lacks the characteristic of arising produce the essence of a phenomenon?

If you hold that there is a jar, then regarding the second point—that which has already arisen from the nature of the dharma—since it already exists, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) cannot produce it.
Within this, there are two further sequences;
regarding the jar, there are two initial [considerations].
The two subsequent "mudrā" (mud) verses reveal the existence or non-existence of the essence of phenomena,
clarifying that the characteristic of arising cannot produce [anything].
Regarding the first of the two types of "beginning of a jar":
first, when a jar has just been completed, it is called the "beginning of the jar.
This already exists and does not require the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) to be produced.
Regarding the second [point], when a jar is first being made, that initial stage is called "the beginning.
This [beginning] lacks the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) and thus cannot produce [the jar].
As for the "second" [stage] of the clay:
First, when the application of clay is completed, it is called "after the clay";
this refers to that which already exists and does not require the arising of further characteristics.
Second, when the work of applying the clay has just begun, it is called "after the clay."
This refers to that which has not yet attained the characteristic of arising and thus cannot produce [an effect].
Furthermore, at the beginning of the text, it is explained that one [precedent] comes first and another follows later;
this refers to the initial formation of a jar and the completion of the process of preparing the clay.
Examining the arising of the jar through these two gateways,
the second section further considers the point after the clay has been exhausted and the very beginning of the jar's manufacture;
this constitutes the "one that has already arisen" and the "one that has not yet arisen."
Examining the arising of a jar that is [in fact] unarisen involves three parts within the first [section]: first, the restatement;
second, the determination; and third, the refutation.
If you maintain that there is an arising of the jar, then even if it arises, you must admit that there is an "arising of the jar" distinct from the person who perceives it.
At the very moment the jar first arises, two gates are opened; this is the determination.
The "initial stage of the jar" refers to the completion of the jar's formation.
The "time of the jar" means that once it has already become a jar, it is the time of the jar.
Regarding "after the lump of clay," the beginning of the creation of the clay is completed, and this is termed "after the clay."
Regarding the phrase "the time when it is not a jar": since the lump of clay has not yet become a jar, it is called "the time when it is not a jar.
As for the third pair of difficulties concerning the initial descent of the jar, they are divided into two distinct parts.
The first section also has four parts:
first, the citation;
second, the general refutation beginning with "This matter is not so."
Why is this? Below, the formal objection is raised:
"Since the jar has already come into existence, there is no need for a further characteristic of arising.
This explains and establishes the objection regarding the mutual dependence of the beginning, middle, and end.
In this process, the mouth of the jar constitutes the beginning,
the belly of the jar constitutes the middle,
and the base of the jar constitutes the end.
If there were no middle or end, there would be no beginning;
just as if there were no bottom or belly, there would be no mouth.
If there is a beginning of a jar, there must necessarily be a middle and an end.
Since there must be a bottom and a belly whenever there is a mouth of a jar,
the fourth objection is that the jar already exists beforehand.
If [it is argued that the jar arises] after the lump of clay, the second [objection] likewise consists of four [points].
The first section restates [the opponent's position]. This is also incorrect; the second section provides a general refutation.
As for "Why is this so? and below, the third section presents the formal objection.
If the jar lacks a beginning, middle, and end, this explains and resolves the objection.
Since the clay has only just begun to form, the mouth, base, and belly of the jar do not yet exist.
If there were no jar, this would constitute the fourth point of the concluding objection.
Furthermore, the second section below, following the clay, first refutes the arising of a non-existent jar;
it also has three parts.
First, restating the productive cause.
"If, after the lump of clay, [it enters] the second meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
"After the lump of clay" means after the clay has been completely used up.
"At the time of the jar" means:
Since the jar has already been completed after the clay has been fully used, it is called the "time of the jar.
If one refers to the initial stage when it was a lump of clay,
it is called the "beginning of the jar" because one is first about to fashion its base.
This is like when a lump of clay is designated as a "lump of clay" at that time;
subsequently, after the lump [is transformed], the third objection is raised to refute the two [positions].
These two passages are easy to understand.
The opponent says: "Since it arises at the time of arising, there is no fault.
We have already refuted this from two perspectives:
first, that the characteristic of arising, whether already arisen or not yet arisen, cannot produce the essence of a dharma.

Next, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), it is clarified that the characteristics of having already arisen or not yet arisen are incapable of producing [a phenomenon] externally; thus, in order to avoid these two types of "already" and "not yet," the Sarvāstivādins establish that there is arising during the "time of arising.
The Saṃmitīya school frequently employs this principle.
The internal [objection] states: "The time of arising is also like this.
This points out that the time of arising is identical to the times of having already arisen and not yet arisen;
at the time of arising, it has only just begun and is not yet complete.
That which first arises is called "half-existence";
as it is not yet complete, it is "half-emptiness.
Therefore, it remains identical to the states of "already" and "not yet."
The opponent says: "Because it establishes a single meaning.
From the preceding section upward, there have been two question-and-answer exchanges;
the first exchange refuted that which has already arisen and that which has not yet arisen.
Next, the refutation of production at the time of production follows;
thus, the refutation of production in all three times is complete.
Indeed, any discussion of production does not transcend the three periods of time.
Since the principle of arising is exhausted within the three periods of time,
external arguments are defeated and words are rendered powerless to provide a remedy.
One can only establish the perception of a jar as it is presently manifested before the eyes.
This is precisely "arising.
The internal [opponent] says: If that were so, then arising would follow and the formation of the entity would become a single meaning.
It is only when the three phases of beginning, middle, and end are complete that it is designated as "formed."
If this "arising" were established through "establishment," then since establishment occurs later, arising would also occur later.
Since there is no establishment at the beginning or in the middle, there is no arising at the beginning or in the middle.
If there is no arising at the beginning and the middle, then the beginning and the middle do not exist;
because the beginning and the middle do not exist, there is also no establishment.
If there is arising at the beginning and the middle, then the beginning and the middle are established.
This would mean that what is not yet established is called "established," which is a perversion.
Furthermore, if that which is not yet established were to become established, then that which is established would become not yet established;
this too is a perversion.
Furthermore, if there is establishment at the very beginning, it contradicts your previous statement,
for you previously clarified that actual establishment exists for the sake of production.
Moreover, you originally maintained that a jar cannot produce itself and must depend on "production" (utpāda) to produce the jar.
If arising were to occur first, the jar would necessarily follow later;
yet, it is only when the jar is formed that we designate it as "arising.
This implies that the jar exists prior to its arising, with arising occurring only subsequently.
This refers to the production of the jar itself; what does it have to do with the "production of production" (jātijāti) producing the jar?
Furthermore, if one speaks of production while the jar is already manifestly established, [it would be illogical].
Once the jar has been produced,

Therefore, we know that it is not the case that there is no effect because there is no cause. Second, those who maintain that the effect does not exist within the cause claim that the cause is distinct from the effect.
Now, if one seeks an effect such as a clay jar that is distinct from its cause—the clay—it cannot be found.
Therefore, one knows that it is not the case that the effect is non-existent within the cause.
Among the two [contradictory] positions, this is the correct meaning.
How is this known to be so?
Regarding the refutation of the "effect existing within the cause," since one [position] has already been refuted,
it should be understood that the present refutation of the "non-existent effect" refutes its alternative.
There are also three parts to the refutation of the "existent effect."
If one asserts that the effect pre-exists within the cause,
how can its arising and ceasing be refuted?
It is explained that this is because they are not distinct.
If the effect is not different from the cause, then when the effect arises, the cause would not cease.
If the cause is not different from the effect, the cause should not produce the jar.
Because they are not different, there is neither the arising of the effect nor the cessation of the cause.
Commentary on the *Śata-śāstra*, Fascicle Lower, Part One.
